chapter.name: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments

questions.q: Which pairing of a function of government with its meaning is correct, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The executive function is the implementation of the rules and the administration of the country according to them. The other pairings swap the three functions: ensuring rules are followed is judicial and creating rules is legislative.
o: Executive function: implementing the rules and administering the country
Legislative function: making sure that everyone follows the rules made for the country
Judicial function: creating the rules that serve as the framework of the country
Executive function: creating the rules that form the framework of the country

questions.q: The chapter says that if the Head Teacher herself picked the Student Committee, the main weakness would be that
questions.a: Method two leaves most students without a voice. Method one is the one that gives an unwieldy committee, the one-grade problem is the argument of Naghma and Shobha, and the last option describes a failure of election, which is method three.
o: most students would have no role and no way to be heard
the committee would grow too large to reach decisions or manage the work
students of one grade alone would end up on the committee, with no others
students would pick people who could not advocate for their class's needs

questions.q: In the chapter, a 'representative' is a person who
questions.a: The chapter's definition: a person chosen to act or make decisions on behalf of another person or group. The distractors confuse a representative with a lawmaker acting alone, with the judicial function, and with a hereditary monarch.
o: is chosen to act or make decisions on behalf of a group
makes all the rules of a country without asking the people it governs
only checks whether the rules made by others are being followed
is born into the family that rules a country and inherits its throne

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT given in the chapter as one of the roles of a government?
questions.a: The listed roles include law and order, peace and security, relations with other countries, defence, essential goods and services, the economy and welfare. Deciding every citizen's religion is not among them; it belongs to a theocracy, not to the roles listed.
o: Deciding which religion every citizen must follow
Managing the country's relationships with other countries
Taking care of the national defence of the country
Delivering goods and services such as education and healthcare

questions.q: In Sundarpur, the villagers need a committee to look after the street lights, the mid-day meal and the well. Each of the ten lanes votes for one person from its own lane, and the ten chosen people form the committee. Which idea from the chapter does this follow?
questions.a: Choosing one person per lane by voting is the third school method, representation. Letting every villager decide each task is the first method; a nominated committee is the second; family succession belongs to monarchy.
o: Representation: voters choose people to act for them
Direct rule: every villager decides every single task together
Nomination: the village head names his own friends to serve
Hereditary rule: the post passes down within one family only

questions.q: A state government announces that 400 government schools will get a library and a science lab this year. Which role of the government listed in the chapter is this mainly?
questions.a: Libraries and labs in schools are education and infrastructure, which the chapter lists under delivering essential goods and services. The other options are different listed roles that do not fit a school-building scheme.
o: Delivering essential goods and services
Taking care of national defence against attack
Managing relationships with other countries
Maintaining law and order in society

questions.q:
Read the statements about government and representation.
1. In the school example, electing one representative from each grade is called a democratic way of forming the committee.
2. Making the rules, implementing them and ensuring they are followed are all together called the legislative function.
3. A representative is chosen to act on behalf of a group.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: only making the rules is legislative; implementing is executive and ensuring they are followed is judicial.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the school story, electing one representative from each grade was preferred to making every student a member of the committee.
Reason (R): If every student in the school is part of the committee, it becomes difficult to reach decisions and manage implementation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: a committee of the whole school is too unwieldy, so the chapter prefers elected representatives.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with what it shows in Column B.
Column A: 1. Parliament passes a law that every school must serve a mid-day meal.  2. Officials set up kitchens in schools under that law.  3. A court examines a complaint that a school is ignoring the law.  4. Each grade votes for one student to sit on the Student Committee.
Column B: a. Judicial function  b. Executive function  c. Legislative function  d. Choosing representatives by election
questions.a: Making the law is legislative, setting up kitchens under it is executive, examining the complaint is judicial, and voting for a grade representative is election of representatives. The distractors swap executive with judicial or legislative, or mix the election with a function.

questions.q: (a) Name the three options the students finally came to for forming the Student Committee. (b) Which of the three does the chapter call the democratic way, and which would make decisions hardest to reach?
questions.a: (a) Everyone in the school joins; the Head Teacher chooses the students; the students choose representatives by voting. (b) The third (voting for representatives) is democratic; the first (everyone joins) makes decisions hardest.
s: Part (a): the three options named: everyone joins, Head Teacher chooses, students vote for representatives
Part (b): voting is the democratic way and everyone joining makes decisions hardest

questions.q: (a) Define a 'representative'. (b) Gurpreet said a committee from one grade alone would not know the problems of other grades. Explain how electing one representative from each grade fixes this.
questions.a: (a) A person chosen to act or make decisions on behalf of another person or a group. (b) Each grade's representative comes from that grade and speaks for its needs, so every grade's problems reach the committee.
s: Part (a): a person chosen to act or decide on behalf of a group
Part (b): each grade has its own representative who raises its needs on the committee

questions.q: The Head Teacher wanted students to (i) make the rules for the school's tasks, (ii) help implement them, and (iii) ensure they are followed. Name the government function each matches, and say which one forms the framework for running a country.
questions.a: (i) legislative, (ii) executive, (iii) judicial. The rules made by the legislative function serve as the framework for running the country.
s: Names the three functions against (i), (ii) and (iii) correctly
States that the rules made (the legislative function) are the framework for running the country

questions.q: State any four roles that the chapter says a government plays in our lives.
questions.a: Any four of: law and order; peace, stability and security; relations with other countries; national defence; essential goods and services; managing the economy; welfare of the people.
s: Two roles stated correctly from the chapter's list
Two further different roles stated correctly

questions.q: In a school of 1,260 students with 42 sections of 30 students each, one representative is elected by each section. Using this, explain why choosing representatives is a workable way to run a large school, and say how many students each representative speaks for.
questions.a: Each representative speaks for 1,260 / 42 = 30 students. Because a small elected committee of 42 can meet and decide, while all 1,260 together cannot, representation makes government workable and still gives every section a voice.
s: 30 students per representative
Explains that a small elected body can decide where the whole group cannot, yet every section keeps a voice

questions.q: Aarav says, 'It makes no difference whether students elect their committee or the Head Teacher chooses it, because the school's rules get made either way.' Do you agree? Use the school example.
questions.a: No. When the Head Teacher chooses, many students have no role and no way to make their voices heard on what they need. In election, each grade chooses someone it believes will advocate for its needs, so the committee has a mandate from the students.
s: Verdict: disagrees with Aarav
Explains what goes wrong when the Head Teacher chooses (no role, no voice)
Explains how election lets each grade choose an advocate for its needs

questions.q: A state decides that every government school will have a library. Describe in three steps how the legislative, the executive and the judicial functions would each be involved.
questions.a: Legislative: the state's lawmakers pass the rule that schools get libraries. Executive: the education department builds libraries and appoints staff according to it. Judicial: if a school is denied its library, a court ensures the rule is followed.
s: Legislative function: creates the rule or law
Executive function: implements it and administers the work
Judicial function: ensures the rule is followed when it is not

questions.q: Write a five-line story about a village committee for the street lights, in which the villagers choose their members in a democratic way. Show why all villagers do not sit on it.
questions.a: A good story has villagers voting for members from each lane (representation), a committee that acts for them on the lights, and a line saying a meeting of all villagers could not decide or manage the work smoothly.
s: Shows the villagers choosing representatives by voting
Shows the committee acting on the villagers' behalf on the task
Gives the reason why everyone cannot be on the committee: decisions and implementation become difficult

questions.q: A school has 1,260 students in 42 sections of 30 each. Evaluate the three options of the chapter for forming its Student Committee. Give the committee size under the first and third options, state the weakness of the second, and conclude which the school should use.
questions.a: The first method gives 1,260 members, so reaching decisions is difficult. The second method, the Head Teacher's choice, leaves most students without a voice. The third method gives 42 members, one chosen by each section who speaks for it. The school should use the third method, the democratic way.
s: First method: committee of 1,260 and the difficulty of deciding and implementing
Second method: most students have no role or voice
Third method: committee of 42, one chosen representative per section
Concludes in favour of electing representatives
Reason for the conclusion uses the other two weaknesses

questions.q: 'The three functions of government are different jobs, but a country needs all three.' Justify with the help of a law on school meals, showing what could go wrong if any one function were missing.
questions.a: Legislative function: makes the rule on meals. Executive: carries it out through kitchens and staff. Judicial: ensures it is followed. Without the first there is no rule to follow; without the second the rule stays on paper; without the third nobody can make an ignoring school comply.
s: Defines the legislative, executive and judicial functions correctly
Applies each to the school meals law
Shows what goes wrong without the legislative or executive function
Shows what goes wrong without the judicial function

questions.q:
The Student Sports Committee of a school in Pune has nine members, one elected by each of the nine sections of Class 7. It made a rule that every runner must register by 3 pm on Friday. The sports teacher's staff set up the registration desk and prepared the lane lists. Karan was refused a lane for registering at 3:20 pm, so he complained to the Head Teacher, who read the rule and the register. The Committee now suggests that it should also hear such complaints, to save time.
(a) Name the government function each of these three actions resembles: making the rule, setting up the desk, and the Head Teacher examining the complaint.
(b) Which method of forming a committee from the chapter did the nine sections use, and why is it better than the sports teacher choosing nine friends?
(c) Which function is the Head Teacher performing in Karan's case, and why must it stay separate from the body that made the rule?
(d) Should the Committee hear complaints about its own rule? Give one gain and one risk and decide.
questions.a: (a) Legislative, executive, judicial. (b) Election of representatives by voting; each section has a voice, unlike the nominated friends. (c) Judicial; if the Committee judged complaints about its own rule it would be judge in its own case, so a complaint may not be heard fairly. (d) Gain: quicker; risk: the body judges its own rule. A sensible decision keeps judging with an independent person such as the Head Teacher.
s: Part (a): legislative, executive and judicial correctly matched
Part (b): election of representatives, each section gets a voice
Part (c): judicial, and why it must stay separate from the rule-maker
Part (d): one gain, one risk and a decision supported by them

questions.q:
Rampura village has 3,000 adults. To decide on repairing the village road, the head called all of them to the ground. About 1,100 came, argued until night and nothing was decided. A month later each of the 12 wards chose one member by voting. The 12 members met for two hours and decided on the repair.
(a) Which of the chapter's three school methods was tried first, and what went wrong with it?
(b) Which method did the village then use to form the group of 12?
(c) Which government function did the 12 members perform in deciding on the repair?
(d) A villager says, 'Twelve people cannot speak for 3,000, so the whole village should decide everything.' Decide whether Rampura should go back, giving one cost and one benefit.
questions.a: (a) Everyone joins; decisions and implementation became difficult. (b) Election of representatives by voting. (c) They took a decision for the village; this is the legislative (rule-making) function. (d) Keep representatives: a meeting of all gave no decision, while members chosen by voting decided in two hours. The cost is that a villager's voice is only through the member; the answer should weigh speed against being heard.
s: Part (a): the first method, everyone joins; decision-making stalled
Part (b): election of representatives by voting
Part (c): taking the decision as the rule-making (legislative) function
Part (d): a decision with one cost and one benefit using parts (a) and (b)

questions.q: Which of the four key differences between governments does the chapter call the most basic one?
questions.a: The chapter introduces the question of who or what gives the government its authority and power as the most basic difference. The other three are the remaining key differences: formation, parts and functions, and goals.
o: Who gets to decide that 'this is the government'
How the government is formed, and who runs the process
What the different parts of the government are and what each does
What goals and ideals the government is trying to achieve

questions.q: Universal adult franchise in a democracy means that
questions.a: Universal adult franchise grants every citizen above a certain age the right to vote for a representative. Equal treatment is the principle of equality and free expression is the principle of freedom.
o: every citizen above a certain age can vote
every citizen has the right to be treated equally in all matters
every citizen can freely express opinions in public places
every citizen can be appointed as a judge in a court of law

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the fundamental principles of democracy described in the chapter?
questions.a: Equality, freedom and representative participation are principles of democracy. Working only for the prosperity of some families is the chapter's example of a government designed for different goals, not of a democratic principle.
o: Prosperity of only some families
Equality of every person before the law
Freedom to make choices and express opinions
Representative participation through elections

questions.q: According to the chapter, an independent judiciary in a democracy ensures that
questions.a: An independent judiciary protects fundamental rights and sees that laws are followed by citizens and all parts of the government. Making laws is the legislative function, and the other options remove the judiciary's independence.
o: laws are followed by citizens and every part of government
the judges frame the laws that the legislature then has to follow
only ordinary citizens, and not the officials, must obey the laws
the executive can change a court's decision whenever it wishes

questions.q: In which year did women in Switzerland get the right to vote, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says Swiss women got the right to vote only in 1971. 1950 is when India gave universal adult franchise; 1928 and 1848 are other years from the chapter that belong to the UK and to Switzerland's democracy.

questions.q: A textbook of Country Q says, 'Our government exists mainly to increase the wealth of five ruling families.' Which of the chapter's four key differences between governments does this statement describe?
questions.a: A statement about the aim of the government answers 'What is the government working for?' The chapter contrasts India, designed for equality and prosperity for all, with governments designed for some families only.
o: What the government is working for
How the government is formed
Who decides that this is the government
What the different parts of the government are

questions.q: Ria reads that Indian women voted from 1950, while women in Switzerland voted only from 1971. Which idea of the chapter does this comparison best illustrate?
questions.a: The chapter uses exactly these two dates to show that even fundamental principles evolved and that democracies differ in practice. The distractors claim sameness or confuse two different principles.
o: The principles of democracy have evolved over time and differ in practice
Universal adult franchise was identical in all democracies from the start
Freedom of speech is a right found only in the Indian republic
An independent judiciary is the same as universal adult franchise

questions.q:
Read the statements about governments.
1. In a democracy like India the people are the source of authority, while in a theocracy the source is religious belief and the head of a religious institution.
2. In kingdoms, usually someone from within the family continues to rule and decide how the government will be set up.
3. The legislative, executive and judicial functions must always be performed by three completely independent bodies in every government.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says the functions can be performed by totally independent bodies or by the same body, so 'must always' is wrong.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Equality in a democracy includes equal access to facilities like education and health.
Reason (R): Every person in a democracy has the right to choose and elect their representatives.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the right to elect representatives is representative participation, a different principle, so it does not explain equal access to education and health.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) State the four questions that the chapter uses to separate one type of government from another. (b) Which of the four separates India from a government designed only for the prosperity of some families?
questions.a: (a) Who decides that this is the government; how the government is formed; what the different parts of the government are and what they do; what the government is working for. (b) What the government is working for: India works towards equality and prosperity for all.
s: Part (a): the four questions stated
Part (b): the goal question, with India's aim of equality and prosperity for all

questions.q: (a) Name the six principles of democracy described on pages 191-192 of the chapter (three headed principles and three given in side boxes). (b) Which of them is said to protect every citizen's rights and see that even the parts of the government follow the law?
questions.a: (a) Equality, freedom, representative participation (headed principles), and universal adult franchise, fundamental rights, independent judiciary (side boxes). (b) Independent judiciary.
s: Part (a): all six principles named
Part (b): independent judiciary

questions.q: What is a constitution? State how the working of the government is decided in most democracies and how it can be decided in a monarchy.
questions.a: A constitution is a book of fundamental rules of the country. In most democracies the system of government is written in it; in a monarchy it can be decided by the king or queen.
s: Defines the constitution as a book of fundamental rules
Contrasts the written constitution of democracies with the monarch deciding in a monarchy

questions.q: Write the three things the chapter says 'equality' means in a democracy.
questions.a: Every person has the right to be treated equally; everyone has equal access to facilities like education and health; everyone is equal before the law.
s: Equal treatment and equal access to facilities such as education and health (one mark)
Equal before the law (one mark)

questions.q: Use India's example of 1950 and Switzerland's of 1971 to explain what is meant by 'even the fundamental principles of democracy have evolved over time'.
questions.a: India gave every adult the right to vote from the beginning of the republic in 1950, whereas Swiss women got it only in 1971. So the principle of universal adult franchise was not complete in every democracy at the start and developed with time.
s: States both facts: India's vote for all adults from 1950, Swiss women's vote in 1971
Draws the conclusion that the principle developed with time and differs between democracies

questions.q: Tara says, 'If a country holds elections, it automatically follows all the principles of democracy described on pages 191-192.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. Elections show representative participation, but the chapter lists five more principles, and says not all democracies are able to put them in practice; for example women in Switzerland could not vote until 1971 even though it held elections.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Names elections as only one principle, representative participation, among the others (equality, freedom, universal adult franchise, fundamental rights, independent judiciary)
Supports with the chapter's statement that principles are ideals, with the Swiss example

questions.q: A country has this law: 'Only men above 25 may vote, and anyone who criticises the ruler in public is punished.' Show that this country cannot be called one that follows the chapter's principles, naming the principles broken.
questions.a: It breaks universal adult franchise, since women and younger adults are not allowed to vote; it breaks freedom, since citizens cannot express their opinions; it also breaks equality, since people are not treated equally.
s: Universal adult franchise broken: only some adults may vote
Freedom broken: opinions cannot be expressed
Equality broken: not all people are treated alike, so the law cannot follow the principles

questions.q: State (i) the source of authority in India, (ii) the source of authority in a theocracy, and (iii) how a government is usually formed in a kingdom.
questions.a: (i) The people of the country. (ii) Religious beliefs and the head of a religious institution. (iii) Usually someone from within the family continues to rule and decides how the government will be set up.
s: India's authority comes from the people
Theocracy's authority is religious belief and the head of a religious institution
A kingdom usually continues within the ruling family

questions.q: Sundarpur's Ward 9 in Nashik is about to elect its ward member. Show how four of these principles would look in this election: equality, freedom, representative participation and universal adult franchise. Then say why a ward may still fall short of some of them.
questions.a: Equality: every person is treated equally and is equal before the law. Freedom: people express opinions on candidates freely. Representative participation: residents elect the member, who then acts for the ward. Universal adult franchise: every adult resident has one vote regardless of sex, wealth or status. Principles are ideals, which are not always fully put into practice.
s: Equality applied to the election
Freedom applied to the election
Representative participation applied: the ward elects the member
Universal adult franchise applied: every adult gets a vote
Explains that the principles are ideals not always practised

questions.q: Compare a democracy such as India with a kingdom on three of the chapter's key questions: how the government is formed, what the parts of the government are and what they do, and what it is working for. Then analyse which of the three shows the widest gap.
questions.a: Formation: democracy through elections; kingdom, someone from within the family continues. Parts: constitution written in a book in most democracies, whereas the king or queen may decide in monarchy; the three functions may be performed by independent bodies or by the same body. Goals: India works for equality and prosperity for all, while some governments are designed for the prosperity of some families. The widest gap is argued, for example the goals.
s: Formation compared
Parts and functions compared, with constitution against the monarch
Goals compared: all against some families
Chooses one as the widest gap
Gives a reason for the choice

questions.q:
Dhara is a country with 8 crore adults, of whom 4 crore are men. From its first election in 1952 only men could vote; women were given the vote in 1974. Its leaders say, 'We were a democracy from 1952, because we hold elections and have courts.'
(a) Which fundamental principle of democracy was incomplete in Dhara until 1974?
(b) What does the chapter's example of Switzerland add to Dhara's story?
(c) Are the leaders right as it stands, or only partly right? Give reasons.
(d) What percentage of Dhara's adults could vote in 1952, and what does it show about the leaders' claim?
questions.a: (a) Universal adult franchise. (b) Switzerland's women voted only from 1971: principles are ideals that democracies reach over time. (c) Partly right: elections and courts are features, but the principle of universal adult franchise was not met. (d) 4/8 = 50%; half the adults were left out, so the claim is only partly true.
s: Part (a): universal adult franchise
Part (b): the Swiss example linked, principles are ideals reached over time
Part (c): a reasoned partly-right verdict
Part (d): 50 percent, tied to the claim

questions.q:
Two schools in Jaipur are compared. In Trust School, the founding family's trust decides the rules and the timetable, names the prefects and spends the school fund on its own guest house. In Open School, students vote for one representative per class, all grades use the library equally, and any student may write opinions in the school magazine. Trust School's results are better and its decisions are quick.
(a) For each school, say who decides and what the school is working for.
(b) Name two democratic principles visible in Open School and where each appears.
(c) Which of the chapter's four key differences between governments does the spending of the school fund illustrate?
(d) A parent must choose a school. Using the chapter, give your decision and one point on each side.
questions.a: (a) Trust School: the trust decides, and works for the trust's interests; Open School: students share the decision, working for all students. (b) Representative participation: the voting for representatives; freedom: writing opinions in the magazine; equality: equal use of the library. (c) What the government is working for. (d) A decision with a point on each side, for example Open School for democratic principles despite slower decisions.
s: Part (a): the trust against the students as deciders, with the aims
Part (b): two principles named with where each appears
Part (c): what the government is working for
Part (d): a decision with a point for each school

questions.q: In the chapter's Table 9.1 of different forms of democratic government, which country has a single-house legislature, the National Assembly?
questions.a: South Korea has a single house, the National Assembly. India, the USA and Australia each have an Upper and a Lower House, which is the look-alike structure the question tests.
o: South Korea
The United States
The Commonwealth of Australia
The Republic of India

questions.q: In a representative democracy the government is described as 'always accountable'. This means that it
questions.a: Accountability means the government is answerable to the people who have elected it. The other options describe lifelong rule, answering to a court alone, or having no duty to explain, none of which the chapter says.
o: is answerable to the people who elected it
answers only to the highest court of the country
stays in office for life once it has been elected
need not explain its decisions between two elections

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of a parliamentary democracy as described in the chapter?
questions.a: In a parliamentary democracy people elect the legislature and not the executive; ministers are selected from the legislature. The direct election of the executive belongs to a presidential democracy.
o: The people elect the executive directly
Members of the executive are also part of the legislature
The council of ministers works while it has the legislature's confidence
Selected members of the legislature become ministers

questions.q: In India the council of ministers can continue to work only as long as it has the confidence of the
questions.a: The chapter says that in India the council of ministers can continue working while it has the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha is the Upper House and is not the one named; courts and annual votes play no such role.
o: Lok Sabha
Rajya Sabha
Supreme Court
citizens at an annual vote

questions.q: In Country Z, voters elect the president directly every four years. The president picks his own team, who are not members of the legislature, and the president cannot be removed by the legislature withdrawing confidence. Which form of government is this?
questions.a: An executive elected by the people that works independently of the legislature and does not need its confidence is a presidential democracy. Parliamentary democracy has the executive inside the legislature.
o: Presidential democracy
Parliamentary democracy
Direct democracy
Constitutional monarchy

questions.q: A news report says: 'The Prime Minister's government fell after the Lok Sabha withdrew its support.' Which statement from the chapter best explains this event?
questions.a: In a parliamentary democracy the council of ministers is accountable to the legislature and works only with its confidence. The other statements are also true, but they explain a presidential office, the make-up of the houses, or the election interval, not the fall.
o: The council of ministers continues only while it has the confidence of the Lok Sabha
The president does not need the legislature's confidence to hold his or her position
The Lower House is elected by direct voting and is generally the more powerful house
General elections in India take place at regular and fixed intervals of five years

questions.q:
Read the statements about forms of democracy.
1. In a direct democracy, citizens elect representatives who take all the decisions for them.
2. In a parliamentary democracy, the people elect the legislature and the executive separately by direct vote.
3. In the USA, general elections occur every four years.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 3 is correct. Direct democracy has citizens decide directly, not through representatives; and in a parliamentary democracy the people elect the legislature but not the executive.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The USA is a presidential democracy.
Reason (R): In the USA the president must have the confidence of Congress in order to stay in his position.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the president is elected by the people and works independently of the legislature. R is false, since the chapter says a president does not need the legislature's confidence.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each country in Column A with its feature from the chapter's Table 9.1 in Column B.
Column A: 1. India  2. USA  3. South Korea  4. Australia
Column B: a. President as executive with a single-house legislature  b. Prime minister and council of ministers, with Senate and House of Representatives of equal power  c. Prime minister and council of ministers, with a Lower House more powerful than the Upper House  d. President as executive with Senate and House of Representatives of equal power
questions.a: India has a prime minister with a more powerful Lok Sabha; the USA a president with equal houses; South Korea a president with one house; Australia a prime minister with equal houses. The distractors swap the president and prime minister rows or the equal-power and single-house features.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by separation of power? (b) How does Table 9.1 describe the judiciary in India?
questions.a: (a) The three organs of government, legislature, executive and judiciary, work independently and do not interfere in each other's functions. (b) Independent from the executive and the legislature.
s: Part (a): three organs work independently without interfering in each other's functions
Part (b): India's judiciary is independent from the executive and legislature

questions.q: (a) State the interval between general elections in India and in the USA. (b) Why does the chapter say these elections happen at regular and fixed intervals?
questions.a: (a) India: every five years; the USA: every four years. (b) So that people can express changes in their choices, and keep the government accountable.
s: Part (a): five years in India, four in the USA
Part (b): fixed intervals give people a regular chance to express changes in their choices

questions.q: Distinguish the Lower House from the Upper House in the way it is formed and in power. Name both houses of the Indian Parliament.
